### III.3 1D $J_{1}$ - $J_{2}$ model

We next extend our observations on the model non-interacting problem from the previous section to an interacting problem. For this we choose the 1D $J_{1}$ - $J_{2}$ spin $1/2$ Heisenberg model with open boundary conditions [91, 92]

$$ \displaystyle\hat{H}=J_{1}\sum_{i=0}^{L-2}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{i+1}+J_{2}\sum_{i=0}^{L-3}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{i+2}. $$

We use $J_{1}=1$ and $J_{2}=0.5$ (we report energies in units of $J_{1}$ ), which corresponds to a simple exactly soluble point for which the ground state per site energy is $e_{g.s.}=-0.375$ [93, 94]. For the wavefunction, we use a matrix product state (MPS) [30, 82, 31], which can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\psi}(s_{1},s_{2},\ldots,s_{L})=A(s_{1})A(s_{2})\ldots A(s_{L}) $$

where $A(s_{i})$ are $D\times D$ matrices except for the first and last which are are $1\times D$ and $D\times 1$ vectors. The ground state at the exactly soluble point can be written as an MPS of $D=2$ . However, to reflect a more typical optimization procedure (where we do not know what the final structure of the ground-state) we will use an MPS of $D=5$ in the following calculations. Furthermore, as written in Eq. 48, the MPS wavefunction contains redundant variational parameters [30, 82, 31]. Thus we expect $S$ and $H$ to have singularities, which are handled by the diagonal shift $\delta$ in Eq. 12 and Eq. 15.

#### III.3.1 Convergence properties of exact optimization algorithms

We first demonstrate the convergence properties of SR, RGN and the approximate Newton method (equivalently, RGN with $\epsilon=\infty$ ) in the absence of noise for $L\leq 20$ where we can exactly sample the Hilbert space by summing over all configurations. Fig. 5(a) plots the optimization trajectories of SR (dashed) and RGN (solid) and Fig. 5(b) plots the approximate Newton optimization trajectories (solid), for various $L$ with $\delta=0.001$ . We note that the approximate Newton trajectories for $L=16$ (yellow) and $L=20$ (cyan) initially follow that of SR (marked by triangles). This is because the wavefunction is too far from the quadratic region and the approximate Hessian has negative eigenvalues, and our algorithm (see Section II.1) falls back to the SR step. On the other hand, the introduction of $S$ in the RGN matrix $H+S/\epsilon$ (dropping $\delta$ for simplicity) removes the negative eigenvalues and leads to a smoother convergence as seen by comparing Fig. 5(a) and Fig. 5(b).

We note that, for this noiseless case, faster convergence is obtained by the approximate Newton method with SR fallback, than by the recommended RGN update with finite $\epsilon$ when targeting high accuracy. This illustrates the potential for improvement when more sophisticated stepsize control procedures (which can adjust $\epsilon$ [20, 21, 95]) are implemented. However, it should be noted that when stochastic noise is introduced, we expect to always require finite $\epsilon$ to regularize the finitely sampled $H$ which can have negative eigenvalues even when all eigenvalues of the exactly sampled $H$ are non-negative. We also observe that even when the optimal $\epsilon$ is chosen (here $\epsilon=\infty$ corresponding to the approximate Newton update) and the quasi-second order step is taken, the improvement over RGN is a constant factor, rather than a scaling difference, since the convergence rate of both RGN and approximate Newton is at best linear. The fitted exponential parameters $a$ and $n$ from Eq. 41 for the optimization trajectories of SR, RGN, and the approximate Newton’s method are listed in Table 1.

We finally consider the effect of wavefunction expressivity on the sampling requirements of SR and RGN. While the 1-dimensional $J_{1}$ - $J_{2}$ ground-state can be written as an MPS of small bond dimension, this is exceptional to the common VMC scenario, where the wavefunction ansatz does not contain the exact ground-state in the variational manifold. To emulate this, we consider an MPS with bond dimension $D=1$ as the variational state, which does not contain the ground-state. Fig. 8 plots the optimization trajectories of SR (dashed) and RGN (solid) for $L=6$ , $L=10$ and $L=20$ at $\delta=0.001$ . Different sample sizes are labeled by different colors, with $\sigma_{M}/|E_{\rm{g.s.}}|$ plotted as the error bar, and red denotes the result using exact sampling.

We first note that RGN with a small sample size can occasionally obtain wavefunctions with low energy along the optimization trajectory. For instance, in Fig. 8(c), the lowest energy wavefunction corresponds to RGN optimization with 200000 samples (solid blue) at step 25. However, the optimization trajectory does not in fact follow that of the noiseless case, and has a large jump. This suggests that this case is best thought of as optimization from a different starting point (after the jump) and that it is not a reliable strategy to use small sample sizes, as corroborated by the data for other system sizes. Nonetheless, it shows that it can be preferable to choose the optimized wavefunction corresponding to the lowest energy during the optimization run, taking into account the statistical error of the energy, rather than from the last optimization iteration.

We also see that, for both RGN and SR, a stable update requires a much sharper scaling of sample size with $L$ for the $D=1$ MPS, than when the MPS contains the ground state (Section III.3.3). In particular, with the $D=1$ MPS, the sample size requirement for RGN increases from $M=2000$ for $L=6$ , to $M=40000$ for $L=10$ , to $M>1000000$ for $L=20$ ; and for SR it increases from $M<1000$ for $L=6$ , to $M=10000$ for $L=10$ , to $M=100000$ for $L=20$ . This is to be contrasted with the $D=5$ MPS, where the RGN sample size requirement scales mildly with $L$ if $\Delta_{\rm{rel}}$ is in the intermediate to high accuracy regime, and the SR trajectories show a modest dependence on sample size and never become unstable. Furthermore, the sharp sample size scaling with $L$ is also reflected in the increasing energy infidelity of the converged variational minimum with $L$ (i.e., $\Delta_{\rm{rel}}<0.45$ , $\Delta_{\rm{rel}}\approx 0.5$ , and $\Delta_{\rm{rel}}\approx 0.55$ for $L=6$ , $L=10$ , and $L=20$ , respectively).

### III.4 2D $J_{1}$ - $J_{2}$ model

We finally consider the non-trivial 2D $J_{1}$ - $J_{2}$ spin $1/2$ model with open boundary conditions on a $L\times L$ lattice

$$ \displaystyle\hat{H}=J_{1}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle}\vec{S}_{i}\cdot\vec{S}_{j} $$

with $J_{1}=1$ and $J_{2}=0.5$ (we report energies in units of $J_{1}$ ). For the wavefunction, we use the projected entangled pair state (PEPS) [96, 30, 31, 82]

$$ \displaystyle\hat{\psi}(s_{1,1},s_{1,2},\ldots,s_{L,L})=\mathrm{tr}[A(s_{1,1})A(s_{1,2})\ldots A(s_{L,L})] $$

where $A(s)$ are $D\times D\times D\times D$ tensors at each site of the lattice and the trace is over all common tensor indices according to the bonds of the lattice. Similar to the MPS wavefunction, the PEPS wavefunction also contains redundant parameters. Therefore, we use a diagonal shift of $\delta=0.001$ to remove singularities when inverting Eq. 12 and Eq. 15 in all the calculations below.

Although the quality of the PEPS ansatz increases as $D$ increases, the ground-state of this model cannot be exactly represented by a PEPS with finite $D$ . Thus the VMC optimization is always over an approximate ground-state manifold, unlike (most of) the simulations in the earlier sections. Therefore, in the following we define $\Delta_{\rm{rel}}=|(E-E_{\rm{min}})/E_{\rm{min}}|$ where $E_{\rm{min}}$ is the variational minimum of the PEPS ansatz.

We finally consider optimizing a PEPS of a fixed $D$ for increasing lattice size. For the $8\times 8$ and $10\times 10$ lattices with $D=8$ PEPS, $E_{\rm{min}}$ are taken from Ref. [98]. Otherwise, $E_{\rm{min}}$ is taken as the converged result with the largest sample size. Note that unlike in the $6\times 6$ lattice, the $D=8$ PEPS does not contain the exact ground-state (to within the achieved statistical error) in these larger lattices. For example, as estimated from Ref. [98], the difference between the $D=6$ and $D=8$ PEPS energies on the $8\times 8$ lattice is $5\times 10^{-5}$ , and for the $10\times 10$ lattice it is $2\times 10^{-4}$ .

Fig. 10 plots the SR and RGN optimization trajectories for the $8\times 8$ , $8\times 10$ and $10\times 10$ lattices with PEPS of $D=8$ . With sufficient samples, RGN optimization clearly converges to the variational minimum much faster than SR. On the other hand, to achieve significant convergence improvement over SR, the required sample size for RGN increases sharply with system size, e.g. 1000 for the $8\times 8$ lattice, at least 5000 for the $8\times 10$ lattice, and 50000 for $10\times 10$ lattice. We note that this observation of sharp sample size scaling is similar to the one made in Section III.3.4 for the $D=1$ MPS, where the accuracy of the ground-state at fixed bond dimension decreases as the system size increases (for small $L$ ). For the 2D $J_{1}$ - $J_{2}$ model, the choice of parameters $J_{2}/J_{1}=0.5$ coincides with a potential gapless ground-state [99, 98], which violates the area law, and thus correctly representing the ground state (to a given fixed energy accuracy per site) is expected to require a PEPS whose bond dimension increases with lattice size.

Fig. 11 plots the SR and RGN optimization trajectories for the $8\times 8$ , $8\times 10$ and $10\times 10$ lattices with PEPS of $D=4$ . These results further confirm our previous observations: to obtain significant RGN acceleration, (i) the $D=4$ PEPS requires significantly larger sample size than the $D=8$ PEPS for the same lattice size, and (ii) the sample size requirement also grows sharply with system size. Finally, comparing the relative convergence rates of SR and RGN for the $D=4$ and $D=8$ cases, we see that the improvement of RGN over SR for a fixed sample size is larger for the more expressive $D=8$ case.

We now summarize our observations in relation to the questions raised in Section II.2 regarding the effect of wavefunction parametrization, wavefunction quality, and system size, on the sample size requirements and performance of RGN and SR updates.

- 1. Due to the intricate dependence of the energy landscape on the variational parameters, as well as the missing contribution from the wavefunction second derivatives, RGN usually cannot be expected to achieve superlinear convergence in energy even without sampling error, as can be seen from, e.g., Fig. 5 for the 1D $J_{1}$ - $J_{2}$ model. Therefore, assuming that both SR and RGN have sufficient samples, although RGN will usually converge more quickly, the number of steps required by SR is expected to only be a constant factor times that of RGN, even as we increase the convergence threshold.

- 2. In the case of the sampling requirements, we first consider the case when the wavefunction ansatz is sufficiently expressive to contain the true ground state. Then, for an efficient RGN update, the sample size requirement is significantly affected by the closeness of the current wavefunction to the ground state (as measured by the relative energy error $\Delta_{\rm{rel}}=|(E-E_{\rm{g.s.}})/E_{\rm{g.s.}}|$ ). When $\Delta_{\rm{rel}}$ is large, the stochastic error in the sampled approximate Hessian determines the RGN performance. Assuming a variance in the eigenvalues $\lambda_{i}(H)$ of $O(L^{2})$ (as we explicitly computed in the noninteracting model, and as seems reasonable in the other lattice models), an efficient RGN update then requires a sample size of $M\sim L^{2}$ , as seen in Fig. 3 for the product model and Fig. 6 for the 1D $J_{1}$ - $J_{2}$ model. As $\Delta_{\rm{rel}}$ decreases, the sample size requirement for an efficient RGN update also significantly decreases, as seen in the major portion of the optimization trajectories for all 3 models studied (Fig. 4(a), Fig. 7, and Fig. 9(d)), until the RGN update becomes limited by the stochastic error in energy. On the other hand, again assuming the wavefunction is sufficiently expressive to contain the true ground state, the sample size requirement for an efficient SR update does not appear to depend on the closeness of the current wavefunction to the ground state (as measured by $\Delta_{\rm{rel}}$ ).

- 3. The sample size requirements for both SR and RGN behave quite differently, however, if the wavefunction ansatz is not sufficiently expressive to contain the exact ground-state. This can be understood in terms of the zero-variance principle, which no longer applies, as well as from the scaling of the variance of eigenvalues $\lambda_{i}(S)$ and $\lambda_{i}(H)$ which may contain additional system size dependence (as explicitly worked out in the noninteracting model). This is numerically demonstrated in Fig. 8 (1D $J_{1}$ - $J_{2}$ model with $D=1$ MPS), where the variational minimum of the ansatz is very far from the ground state. In this case, both SR and RGN require sharply increasing sample size with system size for stable updates. Fig. 9, Fig. 10, and Fig. 11 (2D $J_{1}$ - $J_{2}$ model with PEPS) consider the case when the variational minimum of the ansatz is closer to, but still insufficient to contain the ground state. In this case, the RGN performance strongly degrades if the sample size does not satisfy the required sharp system size scaling, whereas the SR performance has a milder dependence on sample size.

In a practical setting, the most pressing question to answer would be when to choose a first-order or a quasi-second-order method. One way to summarize the information we have gathered is shown in Fig. 12, Fig. 13, and Fig. 14, which use the optimization trajectories computed above to estimate the ratio of the steps $n_{\mathrm{SR}}/n_{\rm{RGN}}$ needed to reach a given energy accuracy $\Delta_{\rm{rel}}=|(E-E_{\rm{min}})/E_{\rm{min}}|$ (measured relative to the variational minimum for the given parametrization), for different numbers of samples $M$ . If we take the cost per RGN step to be roughly 3 times that of an SR step, this ratio corresponds to white in the chosen color scheme. Red then indicates that, for a given $M$ , the total cost of the number of SR steps is less than that of the RGN steps, and green, vice versa. Naturally, we want to use as few samples as possible. Therefore, if the left side of the plot (corresponding to the smallest number of samples) is green, then RGN gives a speedup over SR, otherwise SR should be used.

We see across the cases shown that if the wavefunction is sufficiently expressive, it is always cheaper (in our examples) to use RGN. This is the case for the 1D $J_{1}$ - $J_{2}$ model (Fig. 12) where the variational wavefunction includes the exact ground-state, and also in the 2D $J_{1}$ - $J_{2}$ model for $D=8$ for the smaller lattice sizes (Fig. 14(a)). Once the variational wavefunction becomes less expressive, the leftmost part of the plots is always red, indicating that it is always more cost effective to use SR. Thus, expressivity may be taken as the determining factor for when to use quasi-second-order versus first-order methods. Note that requiring the wavefunction to be expressive is not the same as requiring that we start very close to the ground-state; as we have observed, when the wavefunction is expressive, even when starting far from the minimum, subsequent optimization steps quickly take one into a regime where the RGN update outperforms the SR update. The importance of the expressivity in distinguishing the methods is reminiscent of the strong zero-variance principle of the Linear Method described earlier [20, 19, 88, 21, 89, 2], which achieves an exact step so long as the current wavefunction and space of derivatives contains the exact ground-state.

## V Conclusions

In this work, we investigated the performance of first and quasi-second-order update methods in VMC, represented by the stochastic reconfiguration (SR) and Rayleigh-Gauss-Newton (RGN) methods respectively, across a variety of systems, and with respect to multiple factors, including the sample size requirements of the different algorithms and the dependence on wavefunction quality and wavefunction expressivity. We note that the absence of the expensive wavefunction second derivative, together with the iterative formulation used in this work, mean that the cost of a RGN step is only a small constant factor (e.g. 3 times) larger than that of a SR step with the same sample size. Although the presence of multiple factors led to a somewhat complex analysis (e.g. is it better to perform a noisy RGN step versus a well converged, with respect to sample size, SR step?), the ultimate picture that emerges is simple: (1) quasi-second-order methods achieve faster convergence than first-order methods, but do not achieve second-order convergence in practical settings, but at best a constant factor reduction in the number of steps. (2) Computing a faithful quasi-second-order step carries higher sampling requirements, due to the variance properties of the Hessian. However, quasi-second-order methods benefit greatly from an analog of the zero-variance principle for the Hessian; as shown explicitly in an analytical model, the Hessian variance becomes independent of system size for the exact ground-state. This property of the Hessian manifests rapidly even when starting far away from the ground-state, so long as the wavefunction is expressive enough to contain the ground-state, as the optimization steps rapidly decrease the variance. (3) Because the cost of a well sampled quasi-second-order step is then only a constant factor larger than that of a well sampled first-order step, the (constant) factor faster convergence of the quasi-second-order method wins out. Thus, the primary criterion for when to use a quasi-second-order method is not closeness to the variational minimum (as is the case for deterministic methods), but the overall expressivity of the wavefunction. (4) For sufficiently expressive wavefunctions (i.e. those that include the ground-state in the manifold), quasi-second-order methods thus lead to an overall reduction of cost over first-order methods.

The analysis and conclusions in this work were drawn from specific lattice models and with specific classes of variational states. However, we believe these conclusions extend more broadly, because they reflect the scaling behaviour of SR and RGN with system size, and the Hamiltonians (sums of local terms) and wavefunctions (with product structure) reflect the generic structure of Hamiltonians and wavefunctions of large physical systems. Nonetheless, it is an important future direction to empirically verify these findings in other quantum many-body problems.

More broadly, for wave functions with more than a few thousand variational parameters, genuine second-order methods have seen only limited usage in VMC calculations so far due to the perception of high cost per sample. In this respect, the development of quasi-second-order methods, which have a similar cost per sample to first-order methods, presents a favorable alternative. However, their practical utility has remained constrained by the substantial sampling requirement. The findings of this work suggest that the high sample requirement of quasi-second-order methods is only an issue if the wavefunction is itself not sufficiently expressive. Given the increasing interest in types of wavefunction ansatz, such as tensor networks and neural network states, that are arbitrarily improvable (and therefore arbitrarily expressive) we therefore see an increasing role for second-order optimization methods. It is also worth noting that our implementation has favoured simplicity and other algorithmic enhancements, for example, related to stepsize control, should be revisited in the large number of parameters setting. Finally, we note that variational quantum algorithms are closely related to VMC, thus the findings of this work are relevant to them also.

## VII Appendix

### VII.1 Iterative solution of linear equation for SR and RGN

Here we briefly recapitulate the iterative solution of the linear equations (Eq. 12 and Eq. 15) for SR and RGN in the stochastic setting with a large number of parameters, following Ref. 66. For SR, we solve Eq. 12 by the MINRES [84, 85] algorithm, where each iteration requires one matrix-vector multiplication between the $S+\delta I$ matrix and update vector $p$ . From Eq. 26, this can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n_{v}}S_{ij}p_{j} \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{n_{v}}\left(\frac{1}{n_{s}}\sum_{\vec{x}}v_{i}(\vec{x})v_{j}(\vec{x})-v_{i}v_{j}\right)p_{j} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{s}}\sum_{\vec{x}}v_{i}(\vec{x})\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n_{v}}v_{j}(\vec{x})p_{j}\right)-v_{i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{v}}v_{j}p_{j} $$

where $n_{v}$ is the number of variational parameters, $n_{s}$ the number of samples (which can be much smaller than $n_{v}$ ), and $v_{i}=\langle v_{i}(\vec{x})\rangle_{|\psi^{2}|}$ . The leading computational cost of the matrix-vector multiplication is $O(n_{s}n_{v})$ , and the overall scaling of the MINRES algorithm is thus $O(nn_{s}n_{v})$ , where $n$ is the number of iterations.

Similarly for RGN, we solve Eq. 15 by the LGMRES [86, 87] algorithm, where each iteration requires one matrix-vector multiplication between the RGN matrix $H+(S+\delta I)/\epsilon$ and $p$ . From Eq. 27, the matrix-vector multiplication $Hp$ can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n_{v}}H_{ij}p_{j} \displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{n_{v}}\left(\frac{1}{n_{s}}\sum_{\vec{x}}v_{i}(\vec{x})h_{j}(\vec{x})\right)p_{j} \displaystyle-\sum_{j=1}^{n_{v}}\left(v_{i}h_{j}+g_{i}v_{j}+ES_{ij}\right)p_{j} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{s}}\sum_{\vec{x}}v_{i}(\vec{x})\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n_{v}}h_{j}(\vec{x})p_{j}\right) \displaystyle-v_{i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{v}}h_{j}p_{j}-g_{i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{v}}v_{j}p_{j}-E\sum_{j=1}^{n_{v}}S_{ij}p_{j} $$

where $h_{j}=\langle h_{j}(\vec{x})\rangle_{|\psi^{2}|}$ and matrix-vector multiplication $Sp$ can be computed as in Eq. 51. The dominant scaling of the LGMRES algorithm is thus $O(kmn_{s}n_{v})$ , where $k$ is the number of restarts, and $m$ the size of the Krylov subspace, assuming $m\ll n_{s}$ .

### VII.2 Model exact variances

Here we provide analytical expressions for the variance $\sigma^{2}[E]$ , $\sigma^{2}[g_{i}]$ , $\sigma^{2}[S_{ij}]$ and $\sigma^{2}[H_{ij}]$ of the model problem in Sec. III.2. For the energy

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{2}[E] \displaystyle=\langle E_{L}(x)^{2}\rangle-E^{2}=\sum_{i}\left(1-e_{i}^{2}\right). $$

To compute analytical variances for $g_{i}$ , $S_{ij}$ and $H_{ij}$ , we use error propagation as introduced in Ref. 2. Let $f(\{\bar{y}_{i}\})$ be a function of sampled expectation values $\{\bar{y}_{i}\}$ , and we expand around the exact expectation values $\{\mu_{i}\}$

$$ \displaystyle f(\{\bar{y}_{i}\}) \displaystyle=f(\{\mu_{i}\})+\sum_{i}\partial_{i}f\Delta_{i} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij}\partial_{ij}f\Delta_{i}\Delta_{j}+O(\Delta^{3}), $$

where $\Delta_{i}=\bar{y}_{i}-\mu_{i}\sim O(1/\sqrt{M})$ is the estimated statistical error in the sampled expectation value $\bar{y}_{i}$ with $M$ samples. The sample bias in $f$

$$ \displaystyle\langle f(\{\bar{y}_{i}\})\rangle-f(\{\mu_{i}\})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ij}\partial_{ij}f\langle\Delta_{i}\Delta_{j}\rangle+O(\Delta^{3}) $$

is of order $O(1/M)$ hence can be ignored. The sample variance in $f$

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{M}^{2}[f] \displaystyle=\langle f(\{\bar{y}_{i}\})^{2}\rangle-\langle f(\bar{y}_{i})\rangle^{2} \displaystyle=\sum_{ij}\partial_{i}f\partial_{j}f\langle\Delta_{i}\Delta_{j}\rangle+O(\Delta^{3}). $$

In the following, we define $\sigma^{2}[f]=M\sigma^{2}_{M}[f]$ and ignore the $O(\Delta^{3})$ contribution. Therefore, rewriting Eq. 25 as

$$ \displaystyle g_{i}=f(\bar{y}_{1},\bar{y}_{2},\bar{y}_{3}) \displaystyle=\bar{y}_{1}-\bar{y}_{2}\bar{y}_{3} $$

where $\bar{y}_{1}=\langle E_{L}(x)\nu_{i}(x)\rangle$ , $\bar{y}_{2}=E$ and $\bar{y}_{3}=\langle\nu_{i}(x)\rangle$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{2}[g_{i}]=\sum_{k}\left(1-e_{k}^{2}\right)+O(1). $$

Similarly, from Eq. 26 and Eq. 27, one gets

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{2}[S_{ii}] \displaystyle=\frac{4}{e_{i}^{2}}-4 \displaystyle\sigma^{2}[S_{ij}] \displaystyle=1 $$

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{2}[H_{ii}] \displaystyle=\left(\frac{4}{e_{i}^{2}}-4\right)\sum_{k}\left(1-e_{k}^{2}\right)+O(1) \displaystyle\sigma^{2}[H_{ij}] \displaystyle=\sum_{k}\left(1-e_{k}^{2}\right)+O(1) $$

Here we provide the procedure to obtain Fig. 6. To obtain a wavefunction of a given per site energy, we randomly initialize a MPS of bond dimension $D=5$ . We run imaginary time evolution on the MPS in the form of the simple update method [36] with time step 0.1 for 20 steps, to obtain a state with roughly $\Delta_{\rm{rel}}=6\%$ . We then use VMC with the SR update and adjust $\epsilon$ to obtain the MPS with the desired $\Delta_{\rm{rel}}=5.15\pm 0.05\%$ . We further note that we choose to only sample the $\sum_{i}S^{z}_{i}=0$ sector of the wavefunction in the VMC calculations.

Given an MPS of length $L$ and desired quality, we compute the RGN $\Delta_{M}e=\Delta_{M}E/L$ for increasing $M$ with $\delta=0.01$ and $\delta=0.001$ . Fig. 15(a) shows an example of $L=100$ and $\delta=0.001$ . The data is very noisy due to the singularity in the $S$ and $H$ matrices as a result of the redundant degrees of freedom in the MPS. Furthermore, one cannot analytically compute the exact 1-step $\Delta e$ . Therefore, we use large $M$ to converge the 1-step $\Delta_{M}e$ , which we use to approximate the exact 1-step $\Delta e$ . For instance, in Fig. 15(a), we take $\Delta e$ as the median of $\Delta_{M}e$ for all $M\geq 150000$ , as labeled by the horizontal black line. The data points $(M,\Delta_{M}E/\Delta E)$ are then fitted to the functional form $y=1-b\exp{(-aM)}$ as shown in Fig. 15(b). The fitted functions $y=1-b_{L}\exp{(-a_{L}M)}$ for each $L$ are used to generate Fig. 6.

## Abstract

The prospect of increasing the energy density has promoted research on lithium metal batteries. Yet, avoiding the uncontrolled growth of lithium dendrites and the resulting interfacial instability to ensure the

practical viability of the given battery technology remains a considerable challenge. Here, we report coating the separator with sulfated zirconia superacid to achieve a high lithium ion transference number

of 0.92 and compelling cycle life when a full-cell paired with a LiNi0.82Co0.07Mn0.11O2 cathode was tested in a carbonate electrolyte under practical operating conditions. The exceptionally high transference

number is attributed to strengthened binding of the PF6− anion of the lithium salt with the superacid. Furthermore, a trace amount of water bound to the superacid reacts with PF6− to induce a mechanically

stable solid-electrolyte-interphase (SEI) layer rich in LixPOyFz. This study demonstrates the beneficial effect of the superacid on emerging post-lithium-ion batteries by immobilizing the anion of the salt as

well as modifying the SEI composition.

## Main Text

The emergence and fast growth of the electric vehicle market was enabled by the technological maturity

of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs)1,2. Particularly, a longer driving distance and increased charging speed

played a central role in the widespread adoption of LIBs. Nonetheless, the search for new electrode materials has continued as the energy density of current intercalation-based electrode materials is clearly limited in terms of both their gravimetric and volumetric characteristics. The recent considerable

attention3,4 devoted to lithium metal batteries (LMBs) similarly aimed to increase the energy density as metallic lithium (Li) has a redox potential of −3.04 V vs. the standard hydrogen electrode and a

theoretical specific capacity of 3860 mAh g−1 or 2060 mAh mL–1.

It is well accepted5,6 that the uncontrolled growth of Li dendrites imposes a formidable challenge that would need to be addressed to ensure the reversible and sustainable cycling of LMBs. In particular,

when the charging current surpasses the so-called Sand’s time, the Li-ion concentration at the electrode-

electrolyte interface becomes depleted, thereby allowing dendrites to grow in an accelerated manner7,8.

This phenomenon indicates the importance of uniform and facile Li ion transport near the Li metal

surface, and many reported approaches involving separator coating9-13, surface treatments of Li metal14-

18, and the use of solid electrolytes with high ionic conductivities19-23 can be understood in the same

context. The solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) layer is also well accepted24,25 to play a crucial role in the

interfacial stability during repeated Li plating and stripping. A mechanically weak SEI layer is vulnerable26

to crack formation due to the build-up of stress in the Li deposits underneath. Once the SEI layer breaks down owing to further stress accumulation, the Li deposit could protrude from the layer in the form of

dendritic growth. In addition, it is worth keeping in mind that the cell configurations and manufacturing schemes of existing LIBs are preferred when any new approaches are implemented. In this regard,

carbonate-based electrolytes are desirable27-29 over others because the cathodes to be paired with Li metal electrodes have been developed on the basis of these electrolytes. However, unfortunately, the


<!-- Page 4 -->


Page 4/20

levels of the lowest unoccupied molecular orbitals (LUMOs) of carbonates are sufficiently low30,31 to induce facile reductive decomposition and consequently a weak irregular organic-dominant SEI layer.

Li ion transport in a liquid electrolyte is affected by multiple parameters including salt dissociation,

the degree of solvation, and the viscosity of the solvent, and these parameters are often interrelated to each other. Moreover, Li ion transport and the spatial distribution thereof at the interface are largely influenced by the physicochemical properties of the SEI layer, and the composition of this layer can affect

Li nucleation and subsequent growth behavior32,33. This rationale led us to pursue an approach by which the dissociation of the Li salt is tuned to obtain a high Li ion transference number, and the dissociated anion can yield an SEI layer with high stability upon reaction with the electrolyte solvents. In this vein, we

adopted sulfated zirconia (denoted as S-ZrO2) because S-ZrO2 can function as a solid acid to promote

the dissociation of the Li salt most commonly used in LIBs, namely lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF6),

by strongly binding with the PF6

− anion. A solid acid is a class of superacid and exhibits extremely high

acidity, even several orders of magnitude higher than that of pure sulfuric acid. The extraordinary acidity

of S-ZrO2 arises34,35 from the inductive effect of the sulfate complex with its high electron-withdrawing

ability, which enhances the affinity of the superacid for a Lewis base. We applied a coating of S-ZrO2 superacid nanoparticles to the separator with the aim of distributing the superacid effect over the entire electrode area while simultaneously benchmarking the concept of a ceramic nanoparticle coating to minimize the thermal shrinkage that commercial LIBs are prone to experience at high temperatures. This approach enabled the transference number to reach a value as high as 0.92 as a result of the superacid

effect, and this, along with the modified SEI layer involving liberated PF6

− anions, resulted in highly

reversible and sustainable cyclability of the Li plating-stripping process. In previous studies, solid

superacids were implemented36-38 in polyethylene oxide (PEO) polymer electrolytes to improve the ionic conductivity or transference number; however, they have not been used in liquid-based cells at all. The present investigation points to the unique advantage offered by superacids: simultaneously high values for both ionic conductivity and transference number, unlike solid-state electrolytes that have a high

transference number but are affected by moderate ionic conductivity particularly at the interface, and, needless to mention, poor processability. These beneficial properties are rooted in the physical state of superacid solids; i.e., being solid in nature but functioning in the liquid state.

Synthesis and Coating of Sulfated Zirconia Superacid

The S-ZrO2 nanoparticles were synthesized via a sol-gel process. Briefly, 1.0 M zirconium n-

propoxide in anhydrous n-propanol was hydrolyzed in a mixture of sulfuric acid and distilled water, followed by condensation at 50 °C for 1 hour. The compound in the gel state was washed with anhydrous ethanol and centrifuged to accomplish dehydration. Finally, the centrifuged sample was calcined at 600 °C for 3 hours. Details of the synthetic procedure are provided in the Methods Section. X-ray

diffraction (XRD) analysis (Figure 1a) showed that the synthesized compound had a single tetragonal phase belonging to the P42/nmc space group (ICSD collection code = 66787) without impurities. The

FTIR profile of the S-ZrO2 exhibited peaks at 1213, 1130, 1041, and 995 cm−1 (Figure 1b), which were


<!-- Page 5 -->


Page 5/20

assigned39 to the sulfate ion coordinated to Zr4+ in a bidendate configuration. Thermo-gravimetric analysis (TGA) indicated that the sulfate anion content is 10.0 wt% (Supplementary Figure 1). In addition,

the N2 adsorption-desorption isotherm of S-ZrO2 revealed its surface area to be 104 m2 g−1, and its

primary particle size to be in the range 5−10 nm, as visualized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Figure 1c). After measuring the transference number and assessing the cycling performance with a Li-Li symmetric cell setting by varying the sulfate contents in the range of 2−10 wt% (Supplementary Figure 2),

the sample with sulfate content of 10 wt% was chosen as the main sample for subsequent experiments.

The polyethylene (PE) separator was coated with the prepared S-ZrO2 nanoparticles via a simple

doctor blading process. The coating was uniformly spread across the entire separator (Figure 1d) to obtain a thickness of 3−4 µm (Figure 1e). As in the current LIB technology, the S-ZrO2 coating serves

another purpose namely to ensure the mechanical stability of the membrane against thermal shrinkage. The thermal stability test involved maintaining the separator at 125 °C for 1 hour, and the S-ZrO2-coated

film was observed to preserve 92.6% of its original dimension, in contrast with the 78.7 % retention of the bare PE film (Supplementary Figure 3), indicating that the S-ZrO2 coated separator offers superior

mechanical resistance against high temperature.

Symmetric Cell Test and Electrode Analysis

The effect of the superacid S-ZrO2 on the Li plating and stripping behavior was examined by

conducting galvanostatic tests using a Li-Li symmetric cell configuration. For comparison, cells

containing the bare PE separator and ZrO2-coated separator were also evaluated in parallel. When

scanned at a current density of 3.0 mA cm−2 for 1 hour for each Li plating and stripping, the voltage

profile of the bare PE cell surpassed ±0.4 V after 90 cycles (Figure 2), reflecting40 uncontrolled SEI growth and subsequent electrolyte depletion. The ZrO2-coated cell extended the cycling slightly and began to

surpass ±0.4 V after 96 cycles. After these points of extremely high overpotentials, these two cells ceased to operate. By contrast, the cycling of the S-ZrO2-coated cell was sustained much longer such that its

overpotential surpassed ±0.4 V after 821 cycles. The trend among the cells was translated even when the

current density was raised to 6.0 mA cm−2 for a duration of 0.5 hour for each Li plating and stripping

(Supplementary Figure 4), except that the onset point of voltage fluctuations for the S-ZrO2-coated cell

was dragged to around the 559th cycle owing to the higher current density. In the same context, the S- ZrO2-coated cell exhibited more sustainable cyclability in an asymmetric cell setting in which copper (Cu)

foil was used as one of the electrodes (Supplementary Figure 5).

The effect of the S-ZrO2 superacid coating on the morphology of the Li deposit was investigated

using SEM after the 1st and 100th Li plating when galvanostatically scanned at 3.0 mA cm−2 for 1 hour

for each Li plating and stripping (Figure 3). Even after the 1st charge, the bare PE and ZrO2-coated cells

showed extensive growth of Li dendrites with high aspect ratios according to their top-view images


<!-- Page 6 -->


Page 6/20

(Figure 3a and b, first two images), and the thicknesses of the Li plated layers were 63 and 47 µm, respectively (Figure 3a and b, rightmost images), owing to indiscriminate growth of the SEI layer. By

contrast, the S-ZrO2-coated cell showed a more compact and distributed Li plated layer with rounded

morphology of individual Li deposits (Figure 3c, first two images). The thickness of the Li plated layer

was only 39 µm (Figure 3c, rightmost image). The difference among the cells became more pronounced

after the 100th charge. The growth of sharp Li dendrites continued in the bare PE and ZrO2-coated cells

(Figure 3d and e, first two images), but most of them could barely be observed because of indiscreet coverage by the SEI layer. The uncontrolled growth of the SEI layer was reflected in the significantly

deposit (Figure 3f, first two images), increasing the thickness of the Li plated layer to only 46 µm (Figure 3f, rightmost image). Thus, it can be concluded that the improved cyclability resulting from the S-ZrO2-

coating observed in Figure 2 is associated with the morphology of the Li deposit, which has a direct impact on the interfacial stability.

The reversibility and sustainability of the bare PE, ZrO2-coated, and S-ZrO2-coated cells were also

profiles in their respective 1st cycles in which an average redox voltage of 3.8 V and specific capacity of

mA gcathode

−1), implying that the S-ZrO2 coating on the separator did not alter the full-cell chemistry.

The cyclability of the S-ZrO2-coated full-cell was conspicuously more robust compared to that of the

bare PE and ZrO2-coated full-cells. Upon cycling at 1C (3.0 mA cm−2), the S-ZrO2-coated full-cell

maintained 83.0% of its initial capacity after 150 cycles (Figure 4b), whereas the bare PE and ZrO2-coated

full-cells preserved 25.2% and 23.0% of their initial capacities after the same number of cycles, respectively. The rapid decrease in the capacity of both the bare PE and ZrO2-coated full-cells was also

Origin of High Li+ Transference Number

Raman and 31P solid NMR analyses were carried out to determine the origin of the high Li+

transference number of the S-ZrO2-coated cell. The Raman analysis (Figure 6a) unveils the dissociative

nature of the LiPF6 salt and its interaction with the solvent. This analysis entailed examining the

carbonate electrolyte (1 M LiPF6 in ethylene carbonate (EC) and diethyl carbonate (DEC), 3:7=v:v with 10

vol% fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC)) after soaking the bare PE,  ZrO2-coated, and S-ZrO2-coated

separators in the electrolyte for 24 hours. The Raman spectra of the three samples exhibited similar peak

intensities at 728 cm−1, related46 to Li+−EC interaction, indicating that the solvation environment of the

Li+ ion with EC was not perturbed significantly by the addition of the S-ZrO2 superacid. However, the peak

intensity of the free PF6

− anion at 741 cm−1 relative to that of the free EC peak at 716 cm−1 decreased for

the S-ZrO2-coated separator compared with the bare PE and ZrO2-coated separators (intensity ratio: 0.82

vs. 0.97 vs. 0.94). This observation reveals the Lewis acid-base interaction between the S-ZrO2 superacid

and PF6

−, providing the reason for the increased Li+ ion transference number in the case of the S-ZrO2-

coated separator. In a similar context, the 31P solid NMR spectrum of the S-ZrO2 soaked in the electrolyte

exhibited a band in the range −10 ~ −30 ppm corresponding to the POyF6−y

δ− anion47, which was barely

observed for the ZrO2 counterpart and was not observed at all for bare LiPF6. The appearance of this

band is attributed to the reaction of the PF6

− anion bound to S-ZrO2 with a trace amount of water. This

role of the S-ZrO2 superacid is indeed analogous to the way in which S-ZrO2 offers superacidity: the Lewis

acid sites in the S-ZrO2 superacid attract electron-donating groups (Supplementary Figure 7).

Effect of Sulfated Zirconia on the SEI Properties

The modified potentiostatic intermittent titration (PITT) technique was employed to examine the

electrolyte decomposition behavior at different potentials below the Li/Li+ standard potential (Figure 6c). This analysis was conducted by decreasing the potential in decrements of 2 mV and maintaining the potential at each decremental level for 1 hour to record the electron consumption. In both cells, electrolyte

decomposition was observed in the potential range of −8 ~ −30 mV vs. Li/Li+ before Li deposition was detected below −32 mV with far greater electron consumption. Notably, the amount of electron consumption used for electrolyte decomposition was substantially larger for the S-ZrO2-coated cell

compared with the bare PE cell, revealing that SEI formation was more prominent in the S-ZrO2-coated

cell at higher potentials. Computational calculations were conducted to elucidate the augmented SEI formation in the S-ZrO2-coated cell (Figure 6d). We estimated the energy levels of the lowest unoccupied

molecular orbital (LUMO) of the PF6

− anion, its derivatives upon reaction with water (i.e., POxFy), and the

carbonate solvents included in the electrolyte. According to the results, the first oxidized form of PF6

−,

POF3, has a lower LUMO energy level compared to those of the carbonate solvents. Considering that the

LUMO energy level generally represents a reduction priority, our results suggested that the POF3 formed at

the surface of S-ZrO2 serves as the origin of the prominent electrolyte decomposition of the S-ZrO2-

coated case.

Furthermore, the onset potential for Li deposition was approximately 14 mV higher for the S-ZrO2-

coated cell compared with the bare PE cell (−32 vs. −46 mV) (Figure 6c), inferring48,49 that the modified SEI layer lowers the activation energy for Li deposition. Additionally, the SEI layer of the S-ZrO2-coated cell

proved to be more robust than that of the bare PE cell (Supplementary Figure 8). When the symmetric cells were left standing for a different number of days after one cycle of Li plating and stripping, the increase in the semicircle of the EIS profile was much more prominent for the bare PE cell (Supplementary Figure 8a) compared with that of the S-ZrO2-coated cell (Supplementary Figure 8b), pointing to inferior

SEI stability in the bare PE case.

The effect of the S-ZrO2 superacid on the SEI composition was studied by X-ray photoelectron

spectroscopy (XPS). The XPS spectra of the S-ZrO2 superacid before and after its immersion in the

electrolyte for 24 hours were compared for the Zr 3d, O 1s, S 2p, P 2p, and F 1s branches (Supplementary Figure 9). After immersion, new peaks appeared at higher binding energies of 187.6, 533.5, and 170.8 eV

in the Zr 3d, O 1s, and S 2p branches, respectively, which could likely be attributed to Zr−POyFz, P−O−F50,

and S−O in the sulfate. However, further investigation is needed as the peaks at 187.6 and 170.8 eV were unidentified in the literature. At the same time, a combined analysis of the profiles in the P 2p and F 1s

branches indicates the formation of POyFz

−, which is once again commensurate with the aforementioned

observation related to the reaction of a trace amount of water with PF6

− bound to the S-ZrO2 superacid.

When XPS analysis preceded by 300 seconds of etching was performed for Li metal electrodes after the

1st Li plating (Supplementary Figure 10), the peak of the F 1s branch appeared at 687.2 eV and the peaks

of the P 2p branch were observed at 136.2 and 134.1 eV. This revealed an SEI composition containing LixPOyFz, which is consistent with that of the immersed S-ZrO2 superacid described above, along with the

fact that the interior of the SEI layer is rich in inorganic components. It should be noted that the complete removal of trace water from most carbonate electrolytes is impossible. In our experiment, the formation

POyFz-rich SEI layer.

## Conclusion

Interfacial stability is of key importance for the reliable operation of Li metal anodes and is greatly

affected by the Li ion transference number and SEI characteristics. In spite of the widely accepted consensus in this regard, achieving the desired properties related to these parameters without sacrificing the volumetric energy density is no trivial matter; for instance, the integration of additional components that increase the Li ion transference number is mostly foreign to the current LIB technology and therefore demerits the use of a Li metal anode after comprehensive evaluation.

In this sense, the approach introduced in the present study, namely the incorporation of the S-ZrO2 superacid, is effective yet realistic because the application of a coating of ceramic material to the separator is being adopted in most of the cells that are currently commercially available. Moreover, the effect of the given approach is substantial as the S-ZrO2 superacid enhances binding with the anion of

the Li salt, which increases the mobility of the Li ion apart from inducing a more stable SEI layer. While

this view of the superacid-anion interaction was supported by Raman and 31P NMR analyses, its outcome was electrochemically validated in both symmetric- and full-cell configurations. Taking a broad perspective, the solid-state nature of the superacid warrants its easy integration into a cell and we thus

foresee the universal applicability of the positive effects of the superacid to a wide range of rechargeable batteries beyond LMBs.

## Methods

Synthesis of sulfated ZrO2 superacid and ZrO2 particles. 70 wt% zirconium n-propoxide (Sigma-Aldrich)

in 20 mL of propanol (Sigma-Aldrich) was first mixed with 62.2 mL of anhydrous n-propanol (99.7% purity, Sigma-Aldrich). To this solution, 1.10 mL of sulfuric acid (99.999% purity, Sigma-Aldrich) and 14.81 mL of distilled water were added sequentially for 10 min at 50 °C until the vortex disappeared. The solution was then aged at the same temperature for another hour. Next, 100 mL of ethanol (≥99.5%, Sigma-Aldrich) was added and the solution was centrifuged at 6000 rpm for 10 min to switch the solvent

from water to alcohol to minimize particle growth during drying and calcination. This washing via


<!-- Page 10 -->


Page 10/20

centrifugation was repeated three times. The produced powder was dried at 80 °C for 12 hours to remove

residual alcohol, followed by calcination at 600 °C for 3 hours to produce the designated crystal structure. For S-ZrO2 with 2 and 6 wt% sulfate, the same procedure was adopted except that 0.28 and 0.55 mL of

sulfuric acid was added, respectively. The bare ZrO2 particles were synthesized based on the same

procedure as S-ZrO2 particles except that sulfuric acid was not added.

Coating of S-ZrO2 and ZrO2 particles on the separator. The PE separator (16 µm thick, Toray) was coated

with the synthesized S-ZrO2 and ZrO2 particles by using the doctor blading technique with 33 wt% S-ZrO2 or ZrO2 solution. The areal loading was 1.0 mg cm−2 in both cases. For the thermal shrinkage test,

separators with dimensions of 4.0×4.0 cm2 were left in an oven at 125 °C for 1 hour and the dimensional changes were measured.

Electrochemical analysis. The symmetric cell tests were conducted by sandwiching various polyethylene separators between two sheets of Li foil (200 µm thick, Honjo Metal Co., Ltd.) and galvanostatically

cycled at 3.0 or 6.0 mA cm−2. Each charge or discharge was continued for 1 hour in the case of 3.0 mA

cm−2 and 0.5 hour in the case of 6.0 mA cm−2. The electrolyte was 1 M LiPF6 in EC/DEC (v/v=3/7) with

10 vol% FEC. The cells that were used for the asymmetric cell tests were prepared by using the same procedure except that one side of the electrodes was replaced by Cu foil. For the full-cell tests, LiNi0.82Co0.07Mn0.11O2 cathodes were fabricated by first preparing a slurry consisting of the active

material, Super P, and poly(vinylidene difluoride) (PVDF) in a weight ratio of 96:2:2 in N-methyl-2- pyrrolidone (NMP). The slurry was cast onto Al foil via the doctor blade method and dried at 120 °C for 12

hours. The areal loading of the active material was 15.5 mg cm−2. The Li metal foil on the anode side was 40 µm thick. The electrolyte was the same as that used in the symmetric cells. The full-cells were pre-

cycled at 0.1C and cycled at 1C (1C=200 mA gNCM

−1) in subsequent cycles. The amount of the electrolyte

was 80 µL for each coin cell. Both symmetric and full-cells were prepared in the form of 2032 coin cells by assembling the anode, cathode, and separator in a dry room. The ionic conductivity of each separator

was assessed by performing EIS analysis, which was carried out in the frequency range of 10−2−106 Hz with an amplitude of 10 mV. The ionic conductivity was retrieved from the x-axis intercept of each profile. The transference number was obtained by monitoring the change in the current when subjected to an

applied voltage based on the following relation41,42:

where ISS is steady state current, I0 is initial current, RSS is steady state resistance, R0 is initial resistance,

and ΔV is voltage applied (5 mV in the current study). Modified PITT analysis was conducted by applying

constant voltage for one hour at every 2 mV while the current was monitored. The measured potential

ranged from 0 to −50 mV vs. Li/Li+. To test the stability of the SEI layer, EIS analysis was performed after

leaving the symmetric cells for a different number of days after undergoing one cycle of Li plating and


<!-- Page 11 -->


Page 11/20

stripping (C-rate=0.1C, capacity of each plating and stripping=3 mAh). These measurements were

recorded in the frequency range of 10−2−106 Hz with an amplitude of 10 mV.

Characterization of S-ZrO2 and ZrO2 particles. XRD (Empyrean, PANanalytic) and FTIR (VERTEX 70,

Bruker) analyses were carried out to characterize the crystal structures and chemical bonds of the S-ZrO2 and ZrO2 particles, respectively. TGA (TG/DTA 6300, PerkinElmer) was used to evaluate the sulfate

content in S-ZrO2. SEM analysis (JSM-7000F, JEOL) was performed to visualize the morphology of the Li

metal deposits on the surface. Raman analysis with a laser excitation wavelength of 532 nm (Senterra Grating 400, Bruker) was carried out for the electrolytes in which the different separators were soaked for

24 hours to monitor the ion-to-solvent interaction. 31P solid NMR analysis (ASCEND, Bruker) was

conducted for the S-ZrO2 and ZrO2 particles soaked in the electrolyte for 24 hours. The conditions for 31P

solid NMR analysis were such that the spinning frequency, dwell time, pre-scan delay, recycle delay, excitation pulse length, and excitation pulse power were 11 kHz, 6.3 msec, 6.3 msec, 0.5 sec, 5.0 msec, and 50 W, respectively. XPS (Scientific K-ALPHA, Thermo Fisher) was used to elucidate the SEI components.

DFT calculation. Geometrical optimizations and energy calculations were performed without symmetry restriction using the B3LYP hybrid density functional implemented in the GAUSSIAN 09 software

package51. The 6-311+G(d, p) basis sets were adopted for all the atoms. Frequency calculations at the same basis sets were performed to determine the nature of a stationary point as a true local minimum.

# Repositioning Proton and Electron Donors in a Family of Proton-Coupled Electron Transfer Mediators

**Authors:** Enric H. Adillon; Alexander Alabugin; Sungchan Kim; Jonas C. Peters

**Affiliations:** Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, 6469California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, California 91125, United States

## Abstract

Reagents for reductive PCET often tether an acid and a reductant with a bridging moiety, lowering the effective molecularity of PCET to substrates. The effect of this connecting group on the thermodynamics and kinetics of PCET, however, is not systematically understood. To interrogate the role of the bridge in a well-defined system, we measured PCET rates from a set of anilinium-appended cobaltocene complexes to a series of aryl ketones. Synthesis of four cobaltocene PCET mediators, including one via late-stage Pd-catalyzed cross-coupling of a cobaltocenium salt, enabled systematic variation of the covalent bridge between the cobaltocene electron donor and anilinium proton donor. Measurements of electron and proton transfer equilibria show that the overall PCET driving force is minimally perturbed. Kinetic analysis establishes that aryl ketone reduction by our PCET mediators proceeds by a concerted mechanism in all cases, despite substantial variations in the thermodynamic coupling. Notably, a complex containing an o-phenylene bridge exhibits the fastest PCET rate despite having the least driving force, a result attributed to stabilizing orbital interactions between the ketone substrate and the cyclopentadienyl ligand of the mediator.

## Abstract

## Abstract

## Introduction

Proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) is ubiquitous in biological redox processes such as nitrogen fixation, cellular respiration, and photosynthesis, and is increasingly exploited in catalytic methods for chemical synthesis. − In recent years, molecular catalysts for PCET (herein referred to as PCET mediators) have emerged as effective tools for the electrolytic reduction of N2, CO2, and unsaturated organic small molecules. Such mediators, upon protonation and reduction, act as well-defined H atom equivalents which can be more reactive and selective than direct electrolysis in acidic media, as shown in Scheme a. In this way, mediated electrolysis can lower the overpotential and improve the Faradaic efficiency of reductive protonation reactions.

*1: (a) Reduction of an Unsaturated Substrate by Use of a PCET Mediator, (b) A Sample of Reported PCET Catalysts and Reagents Containing Sites for Proton and Electron Transfer, (c) Exploration of Bridging Group as a Design Parameter for Cobaltocene- and Anilinium-Derived PCET Electrocatalysts*

One such PCET mediator is an aniline-appended cobaltocene (Scheme a) devised by our group, which effects substrate reduction via concerted proton–electron transfer (CPET) to generate O–H, N–H, C–H, and Ni–H radical intermediates under mild conditions. − In this system, a reduced and protonated Co­(II) state is the key reactive intermediate, with a weak BDFEeff of 37 kcal/mol. Following PCET, protonation and electrochemical reduction of the resulting Co­(III) species turns over the catalytic cycle.

While interest in electrocatalytic PCET mediators is growing, reductive PCET mediators remain particularly few in number. Representative examples of PCET mediators are depicted in Scheme b. Mayer and co-workers have established ruthenium-imidazole complexes as tunable PCET platforms, which have been employed as electrocatalysts by Waymouth and co-workers for the PCET-driven oxidation of propanol to acetone. , Nishibayashi and co-workers are exploring iron and cobalt sandwich compounds as stoichiometric PCET reagents as well as a samarium system equipped with a protic arm that may act as a PCET mediator. , A reduced and protonated Cp*Fe-phenol system shows potency for reducing acetophenone, anthracene, and a molybdenum nitride. Other examples include phenol-appended cobalt and nickel pincer complexes from the Siewert group, and a titanium semiquinone complex from the Baek group; both have been used as stoichiometric PCET donors. − These are just a few relevant instances. −

With respect to PCET mediator design, a reasonable first choice of proton and electron donors for a target PCET reaction can be made on thermodynamic grounds using known redox potentials, acidities, and bond energies. These thermodynamic terms set the driving force for PCET (either H atom addition or abstraction), which in general influences PCET rate via linear free energy relationships. Yet it is not obvious how the connection of the electron and proton transfer subunits will affect the PCET mechanism or its rate. Treating bridge position as a PCET design variable, and obtaining benchmark kinetic data on its effect, serves the growing interest in PCET mediatorsespecially if kinetic activity can be improved at decreased thermodynamic overpotential.

To address this gap, we have synthesized and examined a series of cobaltocene-derived PCET mediators based on our original design (Scheme a), herein differing solely in the covalent bridge (Scheme c). Importantly, this series maintains the same electron and proton-bearing fragments and thereby controls for the anticipated influence of driving force. This allows the intrinsic effect of the bridging group to be isolated. Through determination of the crystal structures, measurements of ET and PT equilibria, PCET kinetics, isotope effects, Hammett parameters, and computational analysis, we quantify the bridging group’s influence on the mechanism and rate of PCET. We find that the PCET rate is relatively insensitive to changes in the bridge but also identify a surprising electronic rationale for how a specific bridge can augment metallocene PCET reactivity: the geometry of the acid can direct donor–acceptor orbital interactions reminiscent of a pericyclic reaction with the substrate, promoting electron transfer. As a result, an ortho-substituted analog, which features the least driving force for the model PCET reaction, reacts most rapidly in contrast to the expected rate-driving force relationship. This finding points to secondary-sphere design (inclusive of the linker) as a means to control activity and selectivity in mediated PCET.

## Results and Discussion

### Synthesis

Our series of phenylene-bridged mediators (discussed herein as [Co(II/III)bridge, N/NH]0/+/2+) was prepared in two steps by a variation of our previously reported route to the p-phenylene isomer (Scheme a). Aryllithium addition to [Cp2Co]­[PF6] followed by abstraction of the ring endohydride from Cp­(η4-CpH-PhNMe2)­Co­(I) with the tritylium reagent [Ph3C]­[BArF 4] (ArF = 3,5-bis­(trifluoromethyl)­phenyl) afforded [Co(III) o,m,p‑Ph, N]­BArF 4 salts. − As necessary, Co­(II) forms of the mediators were prepared by thermolysis of the corresponding Co­(I) diene complexes or by reduction of Co­(III) with sodium amalgam (detailed in the Supporting Information).

*2: Synthetic Routes for the Preparation of (a) [Co o–Ph, N], [Co m–Ph, N], and [Co p–Ph, N] and (b) [Co(III) p−Ph2, N]­BArF 4, (c) X-ray Crystal Structures Listed from Top to Bottom: [Co(II) o−Ph, N], [Co(II) m−Ph, N], [Co(II) p−Ph, N], and [Co(II) p−Ph2, N]*

A parallel mediator synthesis was devised which places the harshest and least chemoselective stepsCp-aryl bond formation and cobalt oxidationahead of coupling to the Brønsted acid. As shown in the route in Scheme b, replacement of the lithioaniline synthons with p-lithiobromobenzene or the complex magnesiate Mg­(PhBr)3LiBu yielded Cp­(η4-CpH-PhBr)­Co­(I), an air-stable Co­(I) diene with an exo aryl bromide. Hydride abstraction afforded the cobaltocenium salt [CpCo­(III)­CpBr]­BArF 4, a highly activated electrophilic substrate for Pd cross-coupling chemistry under aqueous Suzuki-Miyaura conditions. The use of a BArF 4 counterion makes purification straightforward via silica gel chromatography. A key advantage of this new cross-coupling methodology is that it enables late-stage diversification of cobaltocenes with functional groups intrinsically incompatible with organolithium addition to [Cp2Co]+ and oxidation of Co­(I).

In addition to the newly reported o-PhNMe2, m-PhNMe2 and p-PhBr substituted Co­(I) dienes, each metallocene complex has been structurally authenticated by single-crystal X-ray diffraction in the neutral (CoII, shown in Scheme c) and cationic (CoIII, see Supporting Information S4) states. The aryl substituents do not significantly perturb the bond metrics of the cobaltocene fragment. Significant C­(Cp)–C­(Ph) torsional strain is evident in [Co o–Ph, N], while the biphenylene moiety in [Co(II) p−Ph2, N] exhibits slight torsion about the C­(Ph)–C­(Ph) bond.

### Thermochemistry

Relevant thermochemistry of the cobaltocene series was obtained by measurements of the proton and electron transfer equilibria, as illustrated in Figure a. Accordingly, the pK a of each [Co(III), NH]2+ was measured by titration with anilinium acids and quantification of the relevant species’ concentrations by 1H NMR spectroscopy (see Supporting Figure S6). The half-wave potentials were measured by cyclic voltammetry in both the aniline (E 1/2(N)) and anilinium (E 1/2(NH)) protonation states, providing the necessary data to determine the BDFEN–H and the thermodynamic coupling values (ΔE 1/2).

*1: (a) Square scheme of [Co(II), NH]+ with coupling highlighted around the outside of the square. (b) pK a (CoIII)-E 1/2(NH) plot of the set of mediators bracketed by diagonal lines of constant BDFE. (c) Electrochemical (blue, left) and spectroscopic (red, right) measurements plotted as a function of BDFEN–H, demonstrating that coupling and driving force in this series are essentially independent. (d) Cyclic voltammograms of [Co(III), N]+ (blue trace) and [Co(III), NH]2+ with 10 mM [4‑CNPhNH3]­[OTf] (black trace) which exemplify how thermochemical coupling is determined electrochemically. (e) UV–vis spectra of [Co(II) o‑Ph, N] and [Co(II) o‑Ph, NH]­BArF 4, exemplifying how spectroscopic coupling is determined.*

The thermochemical profiles are summarized in Table and depicted graphically in Figure b,c. There are small variations in pK a and E 1/2 across the series, but the spread in the BDFEs is very small (36.5 to 37.2 kcal/mol with an estimated error of ±0.4 kcal/mol). Variation in pK a is compensated for by a proportional change in E 1/2 (and vice versa). The exception is [Co(II) o‑Ph, NH]+, with a BDFEN–H (38.8 kcal/mol) that is modestly higher, likely due to electrostatic and steric interactions unique to ortho substitution. In the absence of a covalent linker, the formal BDFEN–H of a combination of cobaltocene (E 1/2 = −1.33 V) and N,N-dimethylanilinium (pK a = 11.47) is estimated as 38 kcal/mol. ,

While the substitution pattern of the linker has little influence on BDFEN–H, it has a significant effect on the thermodynamic (acid–reductant) coupling, which has been inferred to bias systems toward concerted PCET. , We measure thermodynamic coupling electrochemically as the shift in E 1/2 upon changing protonation state. For example, the thermodynamic coupling for [Co(III) o−Ph, N]+ is shown in Figure d as the shift in E 1/2 from [Co(III) o−Ph, N]+ (blue trace) to [Co(III) o−Ph, NH]2+ (black trace) upon addition of acid, approximately +210 mV. An alternative reporter of acid–reductant coupling can be gleaned spectroscopically as a shift in the visible metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) band upon protonation (Δλmax). Herein we refer to Δλmax, a proxy for orbital coupling between the site of the proton and electron, as the spectroscopic coupling. We illustrate spectroscopic coupling using [Co(II) o−Ph, N], whose UV–vis spectrum (blue trace) is depicted in Figure e. Upon addition of acid to form [Co(II) o−Ph,NH]+ (black trace), the feature at 526 nm shifts to 546 nm. For comparison to the thermodynamic coupling, the spectroscopic coupling is reported in Table . It reflects the sensitivity of the (CoII/Cp) → (Ar π*) MLCT to N-protonation, which deactivates the resonance of the aniline N lone pair into the Ar π system.

For three of the complexes in the series, the thermodynamic and spectroscopic coupling are linearly correlated, reflected by an overlay of the red and blue data points in Figure c. However, [Co o–Ph, N] is a clear outlier, with the strongest thermodynamic coupling and weakest spectroscopic coupling. The divergent coupling behavior in [Co o–Ph, N] arises from its combination of internal electrostatic contacts and steric strain. Ortho substitution leads to particularly close proximity between the two formal charge centers (Co and N) and thus a large observed thermodynamic coupling.

The ortho-disposed groups also induce torsion along the C­(Cp)–C­(Ph) bond axis, which disrupts conjugation between the two π systems, rotates the N lone pair out of alignment with the Ar π system, and destabilizes the phenyl-centered acceptor orbital in the MLCT transition (Figure S103).

### Kinetics

To compare PCET reactivity across this cobaltocene series, we chose the reduction of acetophenone as a convenient model reaction that proceeds via a ketyl radical intermediate to a pinacol coupling product (Figure a). We electrolyzed the cobaltocenium complexes at −1.30 V vs Fc0/+ in the presence of excess acetophenone and tosic acid, confirming that each yield electrocatalytic quantities of pinacol (Table S8). For kinetic analysis using UV–vis spectroscopy, the reactive form of the cobaltocene complexes, [Co(II), NH]­BArF 4, was generated in situ by protonation of [Co(II), N] with one equivalent of [H(Et2O)2]­BArF 4 (Figure b). Acetophenone addition (Figure b, black trace) led to formation of [Co(III), N]+, and the resulting kinetic trace was fit to an exponential decay to obtain a first-order rate constant (k obs, Figure c). Plotting k obs as a function of substrate concentration (Figure d) then allowed us to extract k PCET, the second-order rate constant (Figure e). For each complex we measured k PCET using [D(Et2O)2]­BArF 4 to determine the H/D kinetic isotope effect (KIE). We also measured k PCET for a series of p-substituted acetophenones to determine the Hammett slope (ρ), a measure of charge-transfer character in the PCET transition state (Figure e).

*2: (a) Strategy for determination of the PCET rate constant. (b) UV–vis spectra of [Co(II) m‑Ph, N] (red trace) and [Co(II) m‑Ph, NH]­BArF 4 (blue trace) which decays upon addition of acetophenone (black trace) to yield [Co(III), N]­BArF 4 (green trace) after 30 min. (c) Kinetic trace (absorbance vs time) fit to an exponential decay, characteristic of first-order kinetics in which the slope of the fit line yields the observed first-order rate constant. (d) Plot of the first-order rate constants (k obs) against substrate concentration, yielding the second-order rate constant (k PCET) as the slope of the fit line. With this thermodynamic and kinetic data set, we can probe the mechanism for acetophenone reduction by each complex. First, we consider the ET-PT pathway, but we find it is inconsistent with the observed primary KIEs (1.5–2.1) and can be further ruled out by a thermodynamic exclusionary argument, as the free energy for ET from cobaltocene to acetophenone (ΔG ET ° = 19–23 kcal/mol) is greater than the kinetically inferred barrier heights (ΔG ‡ = 16–17 kcal/mol). Next, we consider the PT-ET pathway, which cannot be ruled out on thermodynamic grounds (e.g., ΔG PT,calc = 14–16 kcal/mol). However, we observe negative slopes for rate–driving force relationships based on PT to the p-substituted acetophenones (i.e., ln­(k PCET) vs ΔG PT,calc), which is inconsistent with a rate-limiting PT step. We conclude CPET is the mechanism consistent with the observed data, as was previously determined for the [Co(II) p‑Ph, NH]+ mediator.

These data demonstrate that the concerted mechanism is conserved across all the bridges. This implies that despite substantial variations in the thermodynamic coupling and the individual PT and ET driving forces available at [Co(II), NH]+, the mode of PCET reactivity is here invariant to the position of the electron and proton donors. In contrast, we have previously shown that modifying the redox subunit from cobaltocene to o-carborane switches the mechanism of the PCET reaction from CPET to ET-PT, pre-empting the carborane’s viability as an electrochemical PCET mediator.

Interestingly, Figure e shows a positive and moderately steep Hammett slope (ρ) for [Co(II) o‑Ph, NH]+, [Co(II) m‑Ph, NH]+, and [Co(II) p‑Ph2, NH]+ (ρ = 1.4, 1.3, 1.1), whereas the slope is negative and shallow for [Co(II) p‑Ph, NH]+ (ρ = −0.3). The variation in ρ shows that the bridge modulates the charge-transfer nature of the PCET transition state. ρ does not correlate with PCET rate in this system, suggesting that ET–PT asynchronicity here is not a strong predictor of reactivity. This finding contrasts examples of oxidative PCET where basic asynchronous (PT-led) mechanisms predominate. −

The distinctive ρ value for PCET from [Co(II) p‑Ph, NH]+ can be rationalized via Bernasconi’s principle of nonperfect synchronization (PNS). Here, the para-phenylene bridge is particularly suited to stabilize the [Co(III), N]+ product state by delocalizing the N lone pair into the π-accepting CpCo(III)­Cp-Ar moiety. This is evident in the crystal structure of [Co(III) p‑Ph, N]­OTf, which features a trigonal planar N-center (∑ ∠CNC = 360°). By comparison, the N-centers are more pyramidal in the para-biphenylene, meta- and ortho-phenylene bridged [Co(III), N]+ complexes (∑ ∠CNC = 357°, 356°, and 341°, respectively). Maximizing the quinoidal resonance contribution requires N to rehybridize from a pyramidal to a fully planar geometry, which lags the fast proton motion. The result is an imbalanced transition state characterized by advanced proton transfer and negative ρ (positive charge buildup on the ketone). − A quinoidal resonance form is unavailable to the meta bridge, and extended π-orbital overlap in the para-biphenylene is frustrated by the biphenyl torsion. The ortho analog is sterically blocked from aligning the N lone pair with the Ar π orbitals. As it remains substantially pyramidal in the [Co(III), N]+ product, the ortho compound undergoes the least rehybridization of the 4 mediators.

We plotted k PCET (to acetophenone) against the available thermodynamic, structural, and kinetic parameters to determine which factors most affect PCET reactivity. Surprisingly, we found poor correlations between rate and component driving forces (pK a and E 1/2), thermodynamic coupling (ΔE 1/2), and Co–N distance (Figures S86–S90). Plotting k PCET against the spectroscopic coupling (Δλmax), we find a modest correlation (R 2 = 0.61) in which stronger coupling tracks with slower rate. A potential explanation for this behavior is that the degree of aniline N­(p)-(Ar π*) orbital overlap encoded in Δλmax correlates with part of the inner-sphere PCET reorganization energy, e.g., the previously discussed rehybridization of N on deprotonation. However, equilibrium exchange measurements of the PCET reorganization energy in such reactive systems are complicated by spontaneous hydrogen evolution, so establishing a direct rather than inferred relationship between reorganization energy and Δλmax is presently challenging.

Plotting the transition-state barrier against PCET driving force (the difference in experimental BDFEN–H and calculated ketyl BDFEO–H) does not show the relationship expected of CPET reactions with structurally similar reactants (Figure a). In the low driving force regime, we expect the slope of the fit line (α) from the plot of ΔG PCET ‡ vs ΔG PCET ° to be approximately 0.5. Rather, three complexes with the same BDFEN–H (within error) measurably differ in their PCET rates, while [Co(II) o‑Ph, NH]+ has the least driving force and yet the fastest rate. Consequently, nondriving force parameters such as vibrational overlap, electronic coupling and reorganization energy are likely the dominant rate-controlling factors for PCET in the series, which is uncommon. Examples of structural studies that intentionally isolate these variables are instructive, but very few in number. ,

*3: (a) Transition-state barrier–driving force relationship for acetophenone reduction by [Co­(II), NH]+. (b) Computed transition state geometries for PCET from [Co­(II) o‑Ph, NH]+ to acetophenone in which the acid directs the substrate toward the Ph group (left) or the Cp group (right). (c) Transition state SOMO, highlighting the orbital interaction of the Cp group with the carbonyl.*

Evidently, the rate-contributing factors for PCET across this series of bridges are not captured by ground state (thermochemical and structural) descriptors of the mediator in the absence of substrate. We employed theoretical models of the transition state (TS) for PCET to acetophenone, using density functional theory (DFT) calculations in ORCA 6 with a def2-TZVPP basis, the TPSSh hybrid functional, and implicit SMD­(THF) solvation. , The computed barrier heights (ΔG calc ‡ = 13–18 kcal/mol) varied more than the experimental barriers (ΔG ‡ = 16–17 kcal/mol), meaning that even at a reasonable level of theory, the precision of the DFT energies does not quantitatively resolve the fine differences in rates. Nevertheless, the transition state geometries offer qualitative insights. For each mediator, we identified transition states in which hydrogen bonding directs acetophenone over the phenylene linker (Figures S98–S101). With the meta-, para- and biphenylene bridges, this is the lowest TS barrier. For [Co(II) o‑Ph, NH]+, however, we identified a preferred TS geometry where hydrogen bonding directs acetophenone over the Cp-face of cobaltocene (Figure b). The o-phenylene bridge is uniquely able to preorganize the substrate over the Cp ring due to its proximity to Co, while Cp-stacking is geometrically inaccessible in the other complexes. The resulting O–CCp distance in the transition state is 2.8 Å, shorter than the computed O–CCp distance in a tight CoIII-succinyl ion-pair implicated as an intermediate in the two-electron PCET reduction of fumarate by [Co(II) p‑Ph, NH]+.

Inspecting the computed transition state SOMO reveals that the carbonyl lies across the face of the Cp ring such that the empty C–O π* orbital overlaps with the half-filled Co–Cp π* orbital. Such an orbital interaction is isolobal with the Diels–Alder transition state (Figure c), contributing to the unexpected transition state stabilization by the o-phenylene bridge. More generally, this could help explain cobaltocene’s apparent ability as an ET mediator, lowering the overpotential for reduction of substrates that are recognizable dienophiles. , Dienophile activation by Brønsted acids is well-known; hydrogen bonding from [Co(II), NH]+ both directs and electronically activates the key orbital interaction. While standard DFT calculations yield an adiabatic description of the ground state surface for PCET, we can anticipate that favorable orbital overlap in the TS maps to a substantially enhanced electronic coupling term (Vel) in a more general nonadiabatic theory of PCET rate. , This is because Vel is proportional to the size of the adiabatic energy gap found at the avoided crossing associated with a PCET reaction.

The imbalance between component ET and PT driving forces has been a recent focal point for PCET, as such polar effects can alter rate without changing the overall driving force. Here, we offer an orthogonal consideration to accelerate PCET, independent of intrinsic driving forces and reagent polarity. Since the distance of PT is relatively short, the acid can be considered as a directing group that favorably orients the electron donor and acceptor. We suggest that the geometry enforced by the bridge on this directing group constitutes a design opportunity for PCET mediators.

The chemically intuitive picture of a direct π*-π* orbital interaction is reinforced quantitatively when changes in electron density at the ortho TS are dissected with the extended transition state-natural orbitals for chemical valence (ETS-NOCV) method (Figure ). With the reactants acetophenone and [Co(II), NH]+ as the charge and spin reference state, the dominant NOCV contributors to the difference density at the TS are the Co → CO charge transfer interaction and the O–H–N hydrogen bond, i.e., the partial ET and PT component interactions of PCET. Comparing the two ortho TS conformations reveals that the strength of H-bonding is conserved while the Cp-stacked charge transfer NOCV is preferentially stabilized by π*-π* overlap and exhibits a greater fraction of formal ET (v k = 0.71 vs 0.61).

*4: Comparison of NOCV acceptor orbitals with corresponding stabilization energies (ΔE k in kcal/mol) and fraction of electron transferred (NOCV pair eigenvalue, ν k).*

## Conclusion

To close, we have interrogated how the connection between a Brønsted acid and reductant influences PCET reactivity in a cobaltocene-derived mediator system. We synthesized a series of anilinium-appended cobaltocene complexes that vary only in the identity of the covalent bridging group. Within this set of PCET reductants, thermodynamic measurements establish that the bridge significantly affects acid–reductant coupling while preserving similar H atom transfer driving force. Kinetic measurements establish that the anilinium-appended cobaltocenes all reduce acetophenone via a rate-limiting CPET step, the rate of which is modestly perturbed and contradicts the anticipated rate–driving force relationship. The bridging group exerts its unexpected influence on rate by preorganizing substrates in geometries that differ in their intrinsic barriers, demonstrating the modulation of PCET kinetics at nearly constant driving force.

## Experimental Section

Detailed procedures for the synthesis of all newly reported compounds, measurements to obtain thermodynamic parameters, kinetic measurements, bulk electrolysis data, and data analyses are found in the Supporting Information. Descriptions of quantum chemical calculations and orbital analyses may be found in the SI, and all pertinent ORCA input files and xyz coordinates are provided in a dedicated TXT document.

# Article

Afﬁnity maturation of SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibodies confers potency, breadth, and resilience to viral escape mutations

# Graphical abstract

## Highlights

d Maturation over months increases potency of SARS-CoV-2 neutralizing antibodies

d Antibody maturation restricts options for viral escape

d Maturation of some antibodies enables neutralization of additional sarbecoviruses

d Antibody-spike structures reveal changes that improve potency and breadth

# Authors

Frauke Muecksch, Yiska Weisblum, Christopher O. Barnes, ..., Pamela J. Bjorkman, Theodora Hatziioannou, Paul D. Bieniasz

Correspondence nussen@mail.rockefeller.edu (M.C.N.), bjorkman@caltech.edu (P.J.B.), thatziio@rockefeller.edu (T.H.), pbieniasz@rockefeller.edu (P.D.B.)

## In brief

SARS-CoV-2 RBD-binding antibodies accumulate mutations over months of convalescence, but how maturation affects antibody properties is unclear. Muecksch et al. analyze 6 groups of clonally related neutralizing antibodies from convalescent donors and reveal that antibody maturation increases afﬁnity, potency, and breadth, and restricts viral escape options. They also identify the structural basis for these improved antibody properties during maturation.
